prompt: When someone praises my expertise more than the situation calls for, I notice a pull to prove it by sharing more detail than I meant to.
If someone states something wrong about my work, I feel a strong urge to correct them with the accurate details.
I can let a skeptical or dismissive comment about my work go unanswered without feeling the need to defend it in detail.
When someone shares something that feels confidential with me first, I feel some obligation to offer something similarly candid in return.
If a new acquaintance does me an unprompted favor, I feel I owe them something in return, including information about my work.
Even when someone is unusually attentive and easy to talk to, I keep the same limits on what I share about my work as I would with anyone else.
When someone asks me a direct, specific question about my work, I feel uncomfortable declining to answer even when I am not sure I should.
In an informal setting, I sometimes vent about deadlines, staffing, or project setbacks to people outside my organization.
I hold the same discretion about work topics in a relaxed, off-site setting that I do in the office.
If someone speaks as though they already know details about my work, I tend to confirm or fill in the gaps rather than question how they know.
When someone offers a rough estimate or range about my work that is off, I feel the urge to correct it with the more accurate figure.
I can discuss a hypothetical scenario related to my work without letting it lead me into specifics I would not otherwise share.

My public-facing profiles (professional networking sites, conference bios, social media) describe my current project or technical focus in enough detail that a stranger could tailor questions around it.
In the past year, I have discussed work specifics with a new contact I could not independently verify, at a conference, online forum, or social event.
